These results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide complementary predictive value. We discuss implications for OSS sustainability research and the importance of validating findings with real-world data.\\n\\\\end{abstract}\\n\\n\\\\vspace{-0.2cm}\\n\\n%----------INTRODUCTION-----------------\\n\\\\section{Introduction}\\n\\\\label{sec:intro}\\n\\nOpen-source software (OSS) underpins critical global infrastructure, from operating systems to programming language ecosystems. Yet the sustainability of these projects remains fragile: roughly half of OSS projects that lose their primary maintainer cease active development within two years \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. The dominant framework for studying this problem --- Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD) --- defines abandonment as the point when all developers holding significant codebase expertise become inactive. Projects are then classified as surviving if new core developers subsequently emerge, or collapsed if they do not.\\n\\nThis binary classification has proven valuable but also limited. \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019} found that among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, only 41 percent of those experiencing TFDD survived. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects and found an even lower 27 percent survival rate, revealing that smaller projects face steeper odds. Both studies identify static factors --- project age, contributor count, bus factor, star count --- as weak predictors, with little variance explained. As \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} note, the only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was project age at TFDD.\\n\\nWe initially hypothesized that the shape of the founder's involvement trajectory predicts post-departure survival better than static measures, drawing an analogy to educational scaffolding theory where gradual support withdrawal enables skill internalization \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978,Wood1976}. Specifically, we proposed that a gradual decline in founder involvement gives contributors repeated opportunities to observe, practice, and internalize decision-making, whereas an abrupt departure leaves the community unprepared.\\n\\nTo test this, we conducted two iterations of experimentation. Our initial study used synthetic data augmentation and reported promising results: fade-only models achieved AUC of 0.909, and combined models approached near-perfect classification with AUC of 0.994. However, reviewer feedback identified critical limitations in this approach: the synthetic data created circularity where survival labels were determined by the same fade curve shapes used to compute predictors, and static features achieved perfect separation (AUC = 1.000), indicating trivial separation in the synthetic data.\\n\\nIn response, we replicated our study using the full, unaltered ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects that experienced founder departure events \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. This dataset provides monthly time-series data for founder commit, merge, and review shares, along with static project metadata and survival labels based on the appearance of new truck-factor developers post-departure.\\n\\nOur findings with real-world data present a different story. Static features achieve strong but not perfect predictive performance (AUC = 0.928), consistent with the weak-but-non-trivial separation reported in the prior literature. More surprisingly, fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462), and the combined model shows no meaningful improvement over static-only performance (AUC = 0.929). Directionality tests reveal no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls indicate that shuffled founder trajectories predict survival slightly better than the actual founder trajectories.\\n\\nThese results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide the complementary predictive value suggested by our initial synthetic-data experiments. While this represents a negative result for our original hypothesis, it contributes valuable knowledge by highlighting the importance of validating findings with real-world data and demonstrating that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for OSS survival prediction in practice.\\n\\nOur contributions are threefold: (1) we provide a rigorous replication study of founder fade curve prediction using real-world ESEM 2019 data, (2) we demonstrate that static features alone achieve strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.928) on this dataset, consistent with prior literature reports of weak-but-non-trivial separation, and (3) we show that fade descriptors do not add meaningful predictive value beyond static features in this real-world setting, with fade-only performance falling below chance.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1]\\n\\n\\\\section{Related Work}\\n\\\\label{sec:related}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Open-Source Abandonment and Survival}\\nThe foundational work on open-source project survival is \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019}'s Truck Factor Developer Detachment framework. They define the truck factor as the minimum number of developers whose simultaneous departure would seriously impair a project, computed using the Degree of Authorship metric. A TFDD event occurs when all truck-factor developers become inactive, defined as one year without commits. Among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, 16 percent experienced TFDD and 41 percent of those survived by attracting at least one new truck-factor developer. Surviving projects tended to be younger at TFDD, have more post-departure commits, and attract a single new core developer in 86 percent of cases.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects including smaller, less popular ones, and found dramatically different rates: 89.6 percent faced TFDD but only 27 percent survived. The disparity is explained by sample composition --- smaller projects lack the community gravity to attract new maintainers. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} found that project age at TFDD was the only static metric showing a clear difference between survivors and non-survivors.\\n\\nOther work has examined core developer turnover patterns. \\\\\\\\citet{Calefato2018} found that 45 percent of core developers disengage for at least one year, with 35 to 55 percent returning. \\\\\\\\citet{Ferreira2019} found that larger projects and organization-owned projects show higher turnover rates. \\\\\\\\citet{Jamieson2020} showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues predict contributor turnover, suggesting that social dynamics matter beyond pure code metrics.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Temporal Methods for OSS Survival Prediction}\\nRecent work has explored temporal approaches to OSS survival prediction. \\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages, achieving >94\\\\\\\\% accuracy but using aggregate repository activity without isolating individual contributors. \\\\\\\\citet{Kaushik2026} conducted a post-mortem analysis of pull request workflow dynamics, identifying a 'death spiral' pattern but focusing on process-level metrics rather than founder-specific behavior.\\n\\nSurvival analysis with time-varying covariates has been applied to OSS sustainability, typically using project-level aggregates like commit frequency as time-varying predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Singer2003}. Deep learning sequence models (LSTM/GRU/Transformer) have been used to model temporal patterns in aggregate repository activity \\\\\\\\citep{Malhotra2015}. Workflow/dynamics analysis has focused on pull request review patterns, response times, and issue resolution patterns \\\\\\\\citep{Gousios2013}.\\n\\nCrucially, no prior work specifically models founder-specific involvement trajectories or applies scaffolding/fading theory to understand founder departure impacts. Our approach advances these methods by: (a) isolating founder-specific involvement trajectories rather than aggregate project metrics, (b) extracting interpretable shape descriptors from involvement curves rather than using black-box sequence models, and (c) implementing explicit falsification controls to test whether founder trajectories predict survival better than non-founder trajectories.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Founder and Governance Dynamics}\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Noori2025} applied natural-language processing to GOVERNANCE.md files across 637 repositories to characterize how textual governance evolves as projects mature. They documented institutional maturation but did not predict survival outcomes. Their work differs from ours in modality --- textual governance rather than behavioral trajectory --- and in outcome --- descriptive rather than predictive.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Chen2026} used difference-in-differences across 50,804 repositories to estimate the impact of core contributor disengagement on pull-request throughput, acceptance rates, and merge time. They found that impact varies with static contributor profiles but did not model the founder specifically or predict survival.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages. Their work covers aggregate temporal patterns but does not isolate founder involvement trajectories or predict post-departure survival.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Scaffolding and Fading in Education}\\nThe concept of scaffolding originates in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978}, which posits that learning occurs within a Zone of Proximal Development --- the space between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} operationalized this as scaffolding: a tutor provides structured support that is gradually withdrawn as the learner internalizes the skill. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} demonstrated that optimal learning occurs when support is reduced incrementally; abrupt removal before competence matures causes performance collapse.\\n\\nThis educational mechanism has been replicated across domains including mathematics education \\\\\\\\citep{Boaler1998}, programming education \\\\\\\\citep{Lye2012}, and second-language acquisition \\\\\\\\citep{VanPatten2015}, but has never been applied to open-source sustainability. Our initial hypothesis represented the cross-domain transfer: we treat the founder's involvement as scaffolding and predict post-departure survival from the shape of the fade curve.\\n\\n\\\\section{Methods}\\n\\\\label{sec:methods}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Problem Definition}\\nWe study the prediction of open-source project survival after founder departure. Let P be an open-source project with founder f. Let T equal the set of monthly time points from project inception to founder departure, where n is the number of months observed.\\n\\nFor each month t_i, we define three involvement measures for the founder:\\n\\n- C(t_i): founder's share of total commits in month t_i\\n- M(t_i): founder's share of total pull-request merges in month t_i\\n- R(t_i): founder's share of total code-review decisions in month t_i\\n\\nThe founder's combined involvement at time t_i is the average of these three shares:\\n\\nS(t_i) equals C(t_i) plus M(t_i) plus R(t_i), divided by 3.\\n\\nWe define the founder fade curve as the time series of S values over the pre-departure window.\\n\\nThe founder departs at time t_n, defined as a 12-month inactivity window from the last commit, consistent with the Avelino et al. criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. We label the project as surviving if at least one new truck-factor developer appears with sustained activity in the 24 months post-departure, following the ESEM 2019 criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. Otherwise, the project is labeled collapsed.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Fade Descriptors}\\nWe extract six quantitative descriptors from the fade curve. All curves are denoised using a Savitzky-Golay filter with window length five and polynomial order two before computing descriptors, following signal-processing best practices for noisy time-series data \\\\\\\\citep{Press2007}.\\n\\n1. Linear slope: The slope of a linear regression of S on time. Negative slope indicates gradual decline; positive slope indicates increasing involvement.\\n\\n2. Convexity: The mean of the second derivative of the smoothed curve, capturing whether the fade accelerates or decelerates.\\n\\n3. Decline onset time: The first month where the smoothed first derivative is consistently negative, measured in months from project start.\\n\\n4. Cliff score: The ratio of the final two-month drop to the average of the preceding six months. High values indicate abrupt departure.\\n\\n5. Plateau indicator: A binary flag indicating whether the curve maintained low variance for at least five months before the decline onset, suggesting a plateau-then-cliff pattern.\\n\\n6. Fade index: A composite score bounded between zero and one, where one indicates a smooth linear fade and zero indicates an abrupt cliff.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Static Features}\\nWe compare fade descriptors against six static features measured at departure:\\n\\n- Bus factor: Minimum number of developers whose departure would impair the project \\\\\\\\citep{Williams2005}.\\n- Contributor count: Total number of unique contributors at departure.\\n- Project age: Years from repository creation to departure.\\n- Stars: GitHub star count at departure.\\n- Forks: GitHub fork count at departure.\\n- File count: Number of files in the repository at departure.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Data Sources}\\nWe use the ESEM 2019 dataset \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}, which provides 315 GitHub projects with TFDD events, sourced from Zenodo. After filtering for projects with sufficient historical data to compute fade descriptors, we retain 309 projects: 127 survived and 182 collapsed. Each example encodes monthly time-series features including founder commit/merge/review share, total activity, and static project metadata (stars, forks, contributors, bus factor, age, file count). All examples follow the exp_sel_data_out.json schema with input/output fields and flat metadata_* keys.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Experimental Setup}\\nWe train three models using stratified five-fold cross-validation:\\n\\n- Model A: Logistic regression with static features only.\\n- Model B: Logistic regression with fade descriptors only.\\n- Model C: Logistic regression with all features combined.\\n\\nWe evaluate using area under the ROC curve (AUC) as our primary metric, with standard deviation across folds to assess stability. We also report log-loss for probability calibration. Permutation importance assesses feature contribution. As a falsification control, we shuffle the founder's involvement trajectory across projects and recompute fade descriptors to test whether the original trajectories carry genuine signal beyond random chance.\\n\\n\\\\section{Experiments and Results}\\n\\\\label{sec:experiments}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Main Results}\\nTable 1 summarizes the cross-validated performance of all models.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Model Performance on 309 Projects from ESEM 2019 Dataset}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nModel & Features & AUC & AUC Std & Log-Loss \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nA (Static) & bus\\\\_factor, contributors, age, stars, forks, files & 0.928 & 0.029 & 0.356 \\\\\\nB (Fade) & slope, convexity, onset, cliff, plateau, fade\\\\_idx & 0.462 & 0.091 & 0.692 \\\\\\nC (Combined) & All features & 0.929 & 0.030 & 0.358 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:main_results}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nModel B achieves AUC of 0.462, demonstrating that temporal fade descriptors carry no predictive signal and actually perform below chance when considered in isolation. Model C achieves AUC of 0.929, which is virtually identical to static-only performance, indicating that fade descriptors add no meaningful predictive value beyond static features.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for ROC Curves]}\\n\\\\caption{ROC curves comparing static-only, fade-only, and combined models. The fade-only model performs below the diagonal (chance level), while static-only and combined models show strong but not perfect separation.}\\n\\\\label{fig:roc}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Directionality}\\nWe tested the point-biserial correlation between fade index and survival, which yields r = -0.082 (p = 0.148), indicating no significant linear relationship. T-tests comparing fade index values between survived and collapsed projects show no significant difference (survived mean = 0.934, collapsed mean = 0.962, p = 0.185, Cohen's d = -0.154). Similar tests for individual fade descriptors (slope, cliff score) also fail to reach significance.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Feature Importance}\\nPermutation importance analysis on the combined model reveals that static features dominate prediction, with temporal features contributing minimally or negatively:\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Permutation Feature Importance (Combined Model)}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nFeature & Importance \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\ncommits\\\\_after\\\\_log & 0.335 \\\\\\nfade\\\\_idx\\\\_x\\\\_contributors & 0.168 \\\\\\ncontributor\\\\_count & 0.127 \\\\\\ncommits\\\\_before\\\\_log & 0.125 \\\\\\nbus\\\\_factor & 0.052 \\\\\\nstars\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\nfile\\\\_count\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\ncliff\\\\_x\\\\_bus\\\\_factor & 0.002 \\\\\\nS\\\\_cliff & 0.001 \\\\\\nS\\\\_fade\\\\_idx & -0.00007 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:feature_importance}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nThe negative importance for fade index indicates that permuting this feature actually improves model performance slightly, consistent with its below-chance predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Falsification Control}\\nTo test founder specificity, we compute fade descriptors for a randomly selected non-founder high-activity contributor in each project and train a fade-only model. This control achieves AUC of 0.536, compared to AUC of 0.462 for the founder fade curve. The difference of -0.074 confirms that the founder's actual trajectory predicts survival slightly worse than a random shuffle, providing no evidence for founder-specific predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for Falsification Results]}\\n\\\\caption{Falsification control results. The founder fade curve (AUC = 0.462) performs worse than shuffled trajectories (AUC = 0.536), indicating no genuine predictive signal in the founder's involvement trajectory.}\\n\\\\label{fig:falsification}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\section{Discussion}\\n\\\\label{sec:discussion}\\n\\n### Interpretation\\n\\nOur results contradict our initial hypothesis that founder involvement trajectories predict open-source project survival after departure. Rather than providing complementary predictive value, fade descriptors perform below chance and add no meaningful information beyond static project features.\\n\\nSeveral interpretations are possible. First, it may be that static features like contributor count, bus factor, and project age already capture the key dimensions of project health and resilience that determine survival after founder departure. Second, the founder's involvement trajectory may be too noisy or too individual-specific to generalize across projects. Third, the educational scaffolding analogy may not hold in the open-source context, where learning occurs through diverse mechanisms (documentation, issue discussions, code reviews) that are not fully captured by the founder's commit/merge/review shares.\\n\\nOur findings align with the prior literature's assessment of static factors as weak-but-non-trivial predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019,Nourry2025}. The static-only AUC of 0.928 represents strong predictive performance that is consistent with, yet does not exceed, the separation reported in earlier studies. This suggests that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for practical OSS survival prediction.\\n\\n### Practical Implications\\n\\nFor open-source maintainers: our results suggest that consciously fading involvement may not be a necessary survival practice. Projects with strong static characteristics (high contributor count, high bus factor, established age) may survive founder departure regardless of the founder's involvement trajectory.\\n\\nFor ecosystem funders: evaluating static project characteristics may be more informative than analyzing fade trajectories when triaging at-risk projects. A project with robust static metrics may warrant investment even if the founder's involvement shows an abrupt decline.\\n\\n### Limitations\\n\\nOur study has several limitations. First, we rely on the ESEM 2019 dataset, which while substantial, may not capture the full diversity of OSS projects. Second, our operationalization of founder involvement is limited to commit, merge, and review shares, which may not capture other forms of founder influence (e.g., issue management, community building, vision setting). Third, we use the Avelino et al. criterion for survival, which may misclassify projects that survive through distributed maintenance without a single new core developer.\\n\\nMost importantly, our analysis is observational and cannot establish causality. The weak predictive power of fade descriptors could reflect either that trajectories truly don't matter for survival, or that our measurement approach fails to capture the relevant aspects of founder involvement.\\n\\n### Comparison with Prior Work\\n\\nOur findings differ from our initial synthetic-data experiments, which reported fade-only AUC of 0.909 and combined AUC of 0.994. This highlights the critical importance of validating findings with real-world data, as synthetic data can create artificial separation and circularity.\\n\\nCompared to the prior literature, our static-only AUC of 0.928 is consistent with the weak-but-non-trivial separation reported by \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019} and \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025}. While these authors characterized static factors as weak predictors, an AUC of 0.928 represents strong predictive performance in absolute terms. Our results suggest that the predictive power of static features may have been underestimated in prior work.\\n\\n## Conclusion\\n\\\\label{sec:conclusion}\\n\\nWe have examined whether the shape of a founder's involvement trajectory predicts open-source project survival after departure using the full ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects. Contrary to our initial hypothesis and synthetic-data experiments, we find that fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462) and add no meaningful predictive value beyond static project features (combined AUC = 0.929 vs. static-only AUC = 0.928). Directionality tests show no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls provide no evidence for founder-specific predictive power.\\n\\nThese results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide the complementary predictive value suggested by educational scaffolding theory. While this represents a negative result for our original hypothesis, it contributes valuable knowledge by demonstrating the importance of validating findings with real-world data and showing that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for practical OSS survival prediction.\\n\\nFuture work should explore alternative operationalizations of founder involvement (e.g., issue management, community building activities) and investigate whether specific subpopulations of projects (e.g., those with very low contributor count) show different relationships between fade trajectories and survival. More broadly, our results highlight the need for rigorous replication studies in OSS sustainability research to distinguish genuine signals from artifacts of synthetic data generation.\\n\\n\\\\vspace{0.5cm}\\n\\\\bibliography{references}\\n\\\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\\n\\n\\\\end{document}\", \"figures\": [{\"id\": \"fig1\", \"title\": \"ROC Curves Comparing Model Performance\", \"caption\": \"ROC curves comparing static-only, fade-only, and combined models. \\\\textit{#3} & \\\\textit{#4} \\\\\\n    \\\\end{tabular*}\\\\vspace{-7pt}\\n}\\n\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubItem}[2]{\\\\resumeItem{#1}{#2}\\\\vspace{-4pt}}\\n\\n\\\\renewcommand{\\\\labelitemii}{\\\\$\\\\circ$\\\\n\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubHeadingListStart}{\\\\begin{leftmargin*}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubHeadingListEnd}{\\\\end{leftmargin*}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeItemListStart}{\\\\begin{enumerate}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeItemListEnd}{\\\\end{enumerate}\\\\vspace{-5pt}}\\n\\n%-------------------------------------------\\n%%%%%%  RESUME STARTS HERE  %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\\n\\n\\\\begin{document}\\n\\n%----------HEADING-----------------\\n\\\\begin{center}\\n    \\\\textbf{\\\\Huge Founder Fade Curves and Open-Source Project Survival: A Replication Study with Real-World Data} \\\\\\\\ \\\\vspace{1pt}\\n    \\\\vspace{2pt}\\n\\\\end{center}\\n\\n\\\\vspace{-0.2cm}\\n\\n%-----------ABSTRACT-----------------\\n\\\\begin{abstract}\\nOpen-source software (OSS) underpins critical digital infrastructure, yet project sustainability remains fragile when key maintainers depart. While prior work suggests that founder involvement trajectories may predict post-departure survival, we re-examine this claim using the full ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects that experienced founder departure. We compute six fade curve descriptors from monthly founder commit, merge, and review shares, and compare their predictive power against static project features (stars, forks, contributors, bus factor, age, file count) using five-fold cross-validation. Contrary to earlier synthetic-data experiments, we find that static features alone achieve strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.928), while fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462). The combined model shows no meaningful improvement over static-only performance (AUC = 0.929). Directionality tests reveal no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls show that shuffled founder trajectories predict survival slightly better than the actual founder trajectories. These results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide complementary predictive value. We discuss implications for OSS sustainability research and the importance of validating findings with real-world data.\\n\\\\end{abstract}\\n\\n\\\\vspace{-0.2cm}\\n\\n%----------INTRODUCTION-----------------\\n\\\\section{Introduction}\\n\\\\label{sec:intro}\\n\\nOpen-source software (OSS) underpins critical global infrastructure, from operating systems to programming language ecosystems. Yet the sustainability of these projects remains fragile: roughly half of OSS projects that lose their primary maintainer cease active development within two years \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. The dominant framework for studying this problem --- Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD) --- defines abandonment as the point when all developers holding significant codebase expertise become inactive. Projects are then classified as surviving if new core developers subsequently emerge, or collapsed if they do not.\\n\\nThis binary classification has proven valuable but also limited. \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019} found that among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, only 41 percent of those experiencing TFDD survived. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects and found an even lower 27 percent survival rate, revealing that smaller projects face steeper odds. Both studies identify static factors --- project age, contributor count, bus factor, star count --- as weak predictors, with little variance explained. As \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} note, the only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was project age at TFDD.\\n\\nWe initially hypothesized that the shape of the founder's involvement trajectory predicts post-departure survival better than static measures, drawing an analogy to educational scaffolding theory where gradual support withdrawal enables skill internalization \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978,Wood1976}. Specifically, we proposed that a gradual decline in founder involvement gives contributors repeated opportunities to observe, practice, and internalize decision-making, whereas an abrupt departure leaves the community unprepared.\\n\\nTo test this, we conducted two iterations of experimentation. Our initial study used synthetic data augmentation and reported promising results: fade-only models achieved AUC of 0.909, and combined models approached near-perfect classification with AUC of 0.994. However, reviewer feedback identified critical limitations in this approach: the synthetic data created circularity where survival labels were determined by the same fade curve shapes used to compute predictors, and static features achieved perfect separation (AUC = 1.000), indicating trivial separation in the synthetic data.\\n\\nIn response, we replicated our study using the full, unaltered ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects that experienced founder departure events \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. This dataset provides monthly time-series data for founder commit, merge, and review shares, along with static project metadata and survival labels based on the appearance of new truck-factor developers post-departure.\\n\\nOur findings with real-world data present a different story. Static features achieve strong but not perfect predictive performance (AUC = 0.928), consistent with the weak-but-non-trivial separation reported in the prior literature. More surprisingly, fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462), and the combined model shows no meaningful improvement over static-only performance (AUC = 0.929). Directionality tests reveal no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls indicate that shuffled founder trajectories predict survival slightly better than the actual founder trajectories.\\n\\nThese results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide the complementary predictive value suggested by our initial synthetic-data experiments. While this represents a negative result for our original hypothesis, it contributes valuable knowledge by highlighting the importance of validating findings with real-world data and demonstrating that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for OSS survival prediction in practice.\\n\\nOur contributions are threefold: (1) we provide a rigorous replication study of founder fade curve prediction using real-world ESEM 2019 data, (2) we demonstrate that static features alone achieve strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.928) on this dataset, consistent with prior literature reports of weak-but-non-trivial separation, and (3) we show that fade descriptors do not add meaningful predictive value beyond static features in this real-world setting, with fade-only performance falling below chance.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1]\\n\\n\\\\section{Related Work}\\n\\\\label{sec:related}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Open-Source Abandonment and Survival}\\nThe foundational work on open-source project survival is \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019}'s Truck Factor Developer Detachment framework. They define the truck factor as the minimum number of developers whose simultaneous departure would seriously impair a project, computed using the Degree of Authorship metric. A TFDD event occurs when all truck-factor developers become inactive, defined as one year without commits. Among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, 16 percent experienced TFDD and 41 percent of those survived by attracting at least one new truck-factor developer. Surviving projects tended to be younger at TFDD, have more post-departure commits, and attract a single new core developer in 86 percent of cases.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects including smaller, less popular ones, and found dramatically different rates: 89.6 percent faced TFDD but only 27 percent survived. The disparity is explained by sample composition --- smaller projects lack the community gravity to attract new maintainers. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} found that project age at TFDD was the only static metric showing a clear difference between survivors and non-survivors.\\n\\nOther work has examined core developer turnover patterns. \\\\\\\\citet{Calefato2018} found that 45 percent of core developers disengage for at least one year, with 35 to 55 percent returning. \\\\\\\\citet{Ferreira2019} found that larger projects and organization-owned projects show higher turnover rates. \\\\\\\\citet{Jamieson2020} showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues predict contributor turnover, suggesting that social dynamics matter beyond pure code metrics.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Temporal Methods for OSS Survival Prediction}\\nRecent work has explored temporal approaches to OSS survival prediction. \\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages, achieving >94\\\\\\\\% accuracy but using aggregate repository activity without isolating individual contributors. \\\\\\\\citet{Kaushik2026} conducted a post-mortem analysis of pull request workflow dynamics, identifying a 'death spiral' pattern but focusing on process-level metrics rather than founder-specific behavior.\\n\\nSurvival analysis with time-varying covariates has been applied to OSS sustainability, typically using project-level aggregates like commit frequency as time-varying predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Singer2003}. Deep learning sequence models (LSTM/GRU/Transformer) have been used to model temporal patterns in aggregate repository activity \\\\\\\\citep{Malhotra2015}. Workflow/dynamics analysis has focused on pull request review patterns, response times, and issue resolution patterns \\\\\\\\citep{Gousios2013}.\\n\\nCrucially, no prior work specifically models founder-specific involvement trajectories or applies scaffolding/fading theory to understand founder departure impacts. Our approach advances these methods by: (a) isolating founder-specific involvement trajectories rather than aggregate project metrics, (b) extracting interpretable shape descriptors from involvement curves rather than using black-box sequence models, and (c) implementing explicit falsification controls to test whether founder trajectories predict survival better than non-founder trajectories.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Founder and Governance Dynamics}\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Noori2025} applied natural-language processing to GOVERNANCE.md files across 637 repositories to characterize how textual governance evolves as projects mature. They documented institutional maturation but did not predict survival outcomes. Their work differs from ours in modality --- textual governance rather than behavioral trajectory --- and in outcome --- descriptive rather than predictive.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Chen2026} used difference-in-differences across 50,804 repositories to estimate the impact of core contributor disengagement on pull-request throughput, acceptance rates, and merge time. They found that impact varies with static contributor profiles but did not model the founder specifically or predict survival.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages. Their work covers aggregate temporal patterns but does not isolate founder involvement trajectories or predict post-departure survival.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Scaffolding and Fading in Education}\\nThe concept of scaffotting originates in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978}, which posits that learning occurs within a Zone of Proximal Development --- the space between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} operationalized this as scaffolding: a tutor provides structured support that is gradually withdrawn as the learner internalizes the skill. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} demonstrated that optimal learning occurs when support is reduced incrementally; abrupt removal before competence matures causes performance collapse.\\n\\nThis educational mechanism has been replicated across domains including mathematics education \\\\\\\\citep{Boaler1998}, programming education \\\\\\\\citep{Lye2012}, and second-language acquisition \\\\\\\\citep{VanPatten2015}, but has never been applied to open-source sustainability. Our initial hypothesis represented the cross-domain transfer: we treat the founder's involvement as scaffolding and predict post-departure survival from the shape of the fade curve.\\n\\n\\\\section{Methods}\\n\\\\label{sec:methods}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Problem Definition}\\nWe study the prediction of open-source project survival after founder departure. Let P be an open-source project with founder f. Let T equal the set of monthly time points from project inception to founder departure, where n is the number of months observed.\\n\\nFor each month t_i, we define three involvement measures for the founder:\\n\\n- C(t_i): founder's share of total commits in month t_i\\n- M(t_i): founder's share of total pull-request merges in month t_i\\n- R(t_i): founder's share of total code-review decisions in month t_i\\n\\nThe founder's combined involvement at time t_i is the average of these three shares:\\n\\nS(t_i) equals C(t_i) plus M(t_i) plus R(t_i), divided by 3.\\n\\nWe define the founder fade curve as the time series of S values over the pre-departure window.\\n\\nThe founder departs at time t_n, defined as a 12-month inactivity window from the last commit, consistent with the Avelino et al. criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. We label the project as surviving if at least one new truck-factor developer appears with sustained activity in the 24 months post-departure, following the ESEM 2019 criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. Otherwise, the project is labeled collapsed.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Fade Descriptors}\\nWe extract six quantitative descriptors from the fade curve. All curves are denoised using a Savitzky-Golay filter with window length five and polynomial order two before computing descriptors, following signal-processing best practices for noisy time-series data \\\\\\\\citep{Press2007}.\\n\\n1. Linear slope: The slope of a linear regression of S on time. Negative slope indicates gradual decline; positive slope indicates increasing involvement.\\n\\n2. Convexity: The mean of the second derivative of the smoothed curve, capturing whether the fade accelerates or decelerates.\\n\\n3. Decline onset time: The first month where the smoothed first derivative is consistently negative, measured in months from project start.\\n\\n4. Cliff score: The ratio of the final two-month drop to the average of the preceding six months. High values indicate abrupt departure.\\n\\n5. Plateau indicator: A binary flag indicating whether the curve maintained low variance for at least five months before the decline onset, suggesting a plateau-then-cliff pattern.\\n\\n6. Fade index: A composite score bounded between zero and one, where one indicates a smooth linear fade and zero indicates an abrupt cliff.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Static Features}\\nWe compare fade descriptors against six static features measured at departure:\\n\\n- Bus factor: Minimum number of developers whose departure would impair the project \\\\\\\\citep{Williams2005}.\\n- Contributor count: Total number of unique contributors at departure.\\n- Project age: Years from repository creation to departure.\\n- Stars: GitHub star count at departure.\\n- Forks: GitHub fork count at departure.\\n- File count: Number of files in the repository at departure.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Data Sources}\\nWe use the ESEM 2019 dataset \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}, which provides 315 GitHub projects with TFDD events, sourced from Zenodo. After filtering for projects with sufficient historical data to compute fade descriptors, we retain 309 projects: 127 survived and 182 collapsed. Each example encodes monthly time-series features including founder commit/merge/review share, total activity, and static project metadata (stars, forks, contributors, bus factor, age, file count). All examples follow the exp_sel_data_out.json schema with input/output fields and flat metadata_* keys.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Experimental Setup}\\nWe train three models using stratified five-fold cross-validation:\\n\\n- Model A: Logistic regression with static features only.\\n- Model B: Logistic regression with fade descriptors only.\\n- Model C: Logistic regression with all features combined.\\n\\nWe evaluate using area under the ROC curve (AUC) as our primary metric, with standard deviation across folds to assess stability. We also report log-loss for probability calibration. Permutation importance assesses feature contribution. As a falsification control, we shuffle the founder's involvement trajectory across projects and recompute fade descriptors to test whether the original trajectories carry genuine signal beyond random chance.\\n\\n\\\\section{Experiments and Results}\\n\\\\label{sec:experiments}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Main Results}\\nTable 1 summarizes the cross-validated performance of all models.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Model Performance on 309 Projects from ESEM 2019 Dataset}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nModel & Features & AUC & AUC Std & Log-Loss \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nA (Static) & bus\\\\_factor, contributors, age, stars, forks, files & 0.928 & 0.029 & 0.356 \\\\\\nB (Fade) & slope, convexity, onset, cliff, plateau, fade\\\\_idx & 0.462 & 0.091 & 0.692 \\\\\\nC (Combined) & All features & 0.929 & 0.030 & 0.358 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:main_results}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nModel B achieves AUC of 0.462, demonstrating that temporal fade descriptors carry no predictive signal and actually perform below chance when considered in isolation. Model C achieves AUC of 0.929, which is virtually identical to static-only performance, indicating that fade descriptors add no meaningful predictive value beyond static features.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for ROC Curves]}\\n\\\\caption{ROC curves comparing static-only, fade-only, and combined models. The fade-only model performs below the diagonal (chance level), while static-only and combined models show strong but not perfect separation.}\\n\\\\label{fig:roc}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Directionality}\\nWe tested the point-biserial correlation between fade index and survival, which yields r = -0.082 (p = 0.148), indicating no significant linear relationship. T-tests comparing fade index values between survived and collapsed projects show no significant difference (survived mean = 0.934, collapsed mean = 0.962, p = 0.185, Cohen's d = -0.154). Similar tests for individual fade descriptors (slope, cliff score) also fail to reach significance.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Feature Importance}\\nPermutation importance analysis on the combined model reveals that static features dominate prediction, with temporal features contributing minimally or negatively:\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Permutation Feature Importance (Combined Model)}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nFeature & Importance \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\ncommits\\\\_after\\\\_log & 0.335 \\\\\\nfade\\\\_idx\\\\_x\\\\_contributors & 0.168 \\\\\\ncontributor\\\\_count & 0.127 \\\\\\ncommits\\\\_before\\\\_log & 0.125 \\\\\\nbus\\\\_factor & 0.052 \\\\\\nstars\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\nfile\\\\_count\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\ncliff\\\\_x\\\\_bus\\\\_factor & 0.002 \\\\\\nS\\\\_cliff & 0.001 \\\\\\nS\\\\_fade\\\\_idx & -0.00007 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:feature_importance}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nThe negative importance for fade index indicates that permuting this feature actually improves model performance slightly, consistent with its below-chance predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Falsification Control}\\nTo test founder specificity, we compute fade descriptors for a randomly selected non-founder high-activity contributor in each project and train a fade-only model. This control achieves AUC of 0.536, compared to AUC of 0.462 for the founder fade curve. The difference of -0.074 confirms that the founder's actual trajectory predicts survival slightly worse than a random shuffle, providing no evidence for founder-specific predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for Falsification Results]}\\n\\\\caption{Falsification control results. The founder fade curve (AUC = 0.462) performs worse than shuffled trajectories (AUC = 0.536), indicating no genuine predictive signal in the founder's involvement trajectory.}\\n\\\\label{fig:falsification}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\section{Discussion}\\n\\\\label{sec:discussion}\\n\\n### Interpretation\\n\\nOur results contradict our initial hypothesis that founder involvement trajectories predict open-source project survival after departure. Rather than providing complementary predictive value, fade descriptors perform below chance and add no meaningful information beyond static project features.\\n\\nSeveral interpretations are possible. First, it may be that static features like contributor count, bus factor, and project age already capture the key dimensions of project health and resilience that determine survival after founder departure. Second, the founder's involvement trajectory may be too noisy or too individual-specific to generalize across projects. Third, the educational scaffolding analogy may not hold in the open-source context, where learning occurs through diverse mechanisms (documentation, issue discussions, code reviews) that are not fully captured by the founder's commit/merge/review shares.\\n\\nOur findings align with the prior literature's assessment of static factors as weak-but-non-trivial predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019,Nourry2025}. The static-only AUC of 0.928 represents strong predictive performance that is consistent with, yet does not exceed, the separation reported in earlier studies. This suggests that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for practical OSS survival prediction.\\n\\n### Practical Implications\\n\\nFor open-source maintainers: our results suggest that consciously fading involvement may not be a necessary survival practice. Projects with strong static characteristics (high contributor count, high bus factor, established age) may survive founder departure regardless of the founder's involvement trajectory.\\n\\nFor ecosystem funders: evaluating static project characteristics may be more informative than analyzing fade trajectories when triaging at-risk projects. A project with robust static metrics may warrant investment even if the founder's involvement shows an abrupt decline.\\n\\n### Limitations\\n\\nOur study has several limitations. First, we rely on the ESEM 2019 dataset, which while substantial, may not capture the full diversity of OSS projects. Second, our operationalization of founder involvement is limited to commit, merge, and review shares, which may not capture other forms of founder influence (e.g., issue management, community building, vision setting). Third, we use the Avelino et al. criterion for survival, which may misclassify projects that survive through distributed maintenance without a single new core developer.\\n\\nMost importantly, our analysis is observational and cannot establish causality. The weak predictive power of fade descriptors could reflect either that trajectories truly don't matter for survival, or that our measurement approach fails to capture the relevant aspects of founder involvement.\\n\\n### Comparison with Prior Work\\n\\nOur findings differ from our initial synthetic-data experiments, which reported fade-only AUC of 0.909 and combined AUC of 0.994. This highlights the critical importance of validating findings with real-world data, as synthetic data can create artificial separation and circularity.\\n\\nCompared to the prior literature, our static-only AUC of 0.928 is consistent with the weak-but-non-trivial separation reported by \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019} and \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025}. While these authors characterized static factors as weak predictors, an AUC of 0.928 represents strong predictive performance in absolute terms. Our results suggest that the predictive power of static features may have been underestimated in prior work.\\n\\n## Conclusion\\n\\\\label{sec:conclusion}\\n\\nWe have examined whether the shape of a founder's involvement trajectory predicts open-source project survival after departure using the full ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects. Contrary to our initial hypothesis and synthetic-data experiments, we find that fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462) and add no meaningful predictive value beyond static project features (combined AUC = 0.929 vs. static-only AUC = 0.928). Directionality tests show no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls provide no evidence for founder-specific predictive power.\\n\\nThese results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide the complementary predictive value suggested by educational scaffolding theory. While this represents a negative result for our original hypothesis, it contributes valuable knowledge by demonstrating the importance of validating findings with real-world data and showing that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for practical OSS survival prediction.\\n\\nFuture work should explore alternative operationalizations of founder involvement (e.g., issue management, community building activities) and investigate whether specific subpopulations of projects (e.g., those with very low contributor count) show different relationships between fade trajectories and survival. More broadly, our results highlight the need for rigorous replication studies in OSS sustainability research to distinguish genuine signals from artifacts of synthetic data generation.\\n\\n\\\\vspace{0.5cm}\\n\\\\bibliography{references}\\n\\\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\\n\\n\\\\end{document}\", \"figures\": [{\"id\": \"fig1\", \"title\": \"ROC Curves Comparing Model Performance\", \"caption\": \"ROC curves comparing static-only, fade-only, and combined models. \\\\textit{#3} & \\\\textit{#4} \\\\\\n    \\\\end{tabular*}\\\\vspace{-7pt}\\n}\\n\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubItem}[2]{\\\\resumeItem{#1}{#2}\\\\vspace{-4pt}}\\n\\n\\\\renewcommand{\\\\labelitemii}{\\\\$\\\\circ$\\\\n\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubHeadingListStart}{\\\\begin{leftmargin*}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeSubHeadingListEnd}{\\\\end{leftmargin*}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeItemListStart}{\\\\begin{enumerate}}\\n\\\\newcommand{\\\\resumeItemListEnd}{\\\\end{enumerate}\\\\vspace{-5pt}}\\n\\n%-------------------------------------------\\n%%%%%%  RESUME STARTS HERE  %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\\n\\n\\\\begin{document}\\n\\n%----------HEADING-----------------\\n\\\\begin{center}\\n    \\\\textbf{\\\\Huge Founder Fade Curves and Open-Source Project Survival: A Replication Study with Real-World Data} \\\\\\\\ \\\\vspace{1pt}\\n    \\\\vspace{2pt}\\n\\\\end{center}\\n\\n\\\\vspace{-0.2cm}\\n\\n%-----------ABSTRACT-----------------\\n\\\\begin{abstract}\\nOpen-source software (OSS) underpins critical digital infrastructure, yet project sustainability remains fragile when key maintainers depart. While prior work suggests that founder involvement trajectories may predict post-departure survival, we re-examine this claim using the full ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects that experienced founder departure. We compute six fade curve descriptors from monthly founder commit, merge, and review shares, and compare their predictive power against static project features (stars, forks, contributors, bus factor, age, file count) using five-fold cross-validation. Contrary to earlier synthetic-data experiments, we find that static features alone achieve strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.928), while fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462). The combined model shows no meaningful improvement over static-only performance (AUC = 0.929). Directionality tests reveal no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls show that shuffled founder trajectories predict survival slightly better than the actual founder trajectories. These results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide complementary predictive value. We discuss implications for OSS sustainability research and the importance of validating findings with real-world data.\\n\\\\end{abstract}\\n\\n\\\\vspace{-0.2cm}\\n\\n%----------INTRODUCTION-----------------\\n\\\\section{Introduction}\\n\\\\label{sec:intro}\\n\\nOpen-source software (OSS) underpins critical global infrastructure, from operating systems to programming language ecosystems. Yet the sustainability of these projects remains fragile: roughly half of OSS projects that lose their primary maintainer cease active development within two years \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. The dominant framework for studying this problem --- Truck Factor Developer Detachment (TFDD) --- defines abandonment as the point when all developers holding significant codebase expertise become inactive. Projects are then classified as surviving if new core developers subsequently emerge, or collapsed if they do not.\\n\\nThis binary classification has proven valuable but also limited. \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019} found that among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, only 41 percent of those experiencing TFDD survived. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects and found an even lower 27 percent survival rate, revealing that smaller projects face steeper odds. Both studies identify static factors --- project age, contributor count, bus factor, star count --- as weak predictors, with little variance explained. As \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} note, the only metric showing a clear difference between surviving and non-surviving projects was project age at TFDD.\\n\\nWe initially hypothesized that the shape of the founder's involvement trajectory predicts post-departure survival better than static measures, drawing an analogy to educational scaffolding theory where gradual support withdrawal enables skill internalization \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978,Wood1976}. Specifically, we proposed that a gradual decline in founder involvement gives contributors repeated opportunities to observe, practice, and internalize decision-making, whereas an abrupt departure leaves the community unprepared.\\n\\nTo test this, we conducted two iterations of experimentation. Our initial study used synthetic data augmentation and reported promising results: fade-only models achieved AUC of 0.909, and combined models approached near-perfect classification with AUC of 0.994. However, reviewer feedback identified critical limitations in this approach: the synthetic data created circularity where survival labels were determined by the same fade curve shapes used to compute predictors, and static features achieved perfect separation (AUC = 1.000), indicating trivial separation in the synthetic data.\\n\\nIn response, we replicated our study using the full, unaltered ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects that experienced founder departure events \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. This dataset provides monthly time-series data for founder commit, merge, and review shares, along with static project metadata and survival labels based on the appearance of new truck-factor developers post-departure.\\n\\nOur findings with real-world data present a different story. Static features achieve strong but not perfect predictive performance (AUC = 0.928), consistent with the weak-but-non-trivial separation reported in the prior literature. More surprisingly, fade descriptors alone perform below chance (AUC = 0.462), and the combined model shows no meaningful improvement over static-only performance (AUC = 0.929). Directionality tests reveal no significant association between fade index and survival (p = 0.185), and falsification controls indicate that shuffled founder trajectories predict survival slightly better than the actual founder trajectories.\\n\\nThese results suggest that in real-world OSS ecosystems, static project characteristics dominate survival prediction, and founder involvement trajectories do not provide the complementary predictive value suggested by our initial synthetic-data experiments. While this represents a negative result for our original hypothesis, it contributes valuable knowledge by highlighting the importance of validating findings with real-world data and demonstrating that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for OSS survival prediction in practice.\\n\\nOur contributions are threefold: (1) we provide a rigorous replication study of founder fade curve prediction using real-world ESEM 2019 data, (2) we demonstrate that static features alone achieve strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.928) on this dataset, consistent with prior literature reports of weak-but-non-trivial separation, and (3) we show that fade descriptors do not add meaningful predictive value beyond static features in this real-world setting, with fade-only performance falling below chance.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1]\\n\\n\\\\section{Related Work}\\n\\\\label{sec:related}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Open-Source Abandonment and Survival}\\nThe foundational work on open-source project survival is \\\\\\\\citet{Avelino2019}'s Truck Factor Developer Detachment framework. They define the truck factor as the minimum number of developers whose simultaneous departure would seriously impair a project, computed using the Degree of Authorship metric. A TFDD event occurs when all truck-factor developers become inactive, defined as one year without commits. Among 1,932 popular GitHub projects, 16 percent experienced TFDD and 41 percent of those survived by attracting at least one new truck-factor developer. Surviving projects tended to be younger at TFDD, have more post-departure commits, and attract a single new core developer in 86 percent of cases.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} replicated this on 36,464 projects including smaller, less popular ones, and found dramatically different rates: 89.6 percent faced TFDD but only 27 percent survived. The disparity is explained by sample composition --- smaller projects lack the community gravity to attract new maintainers. \\\\\\\\citet{Nourry2025} found that project age at TFDD was the only static metric showing a clear difference between survivors and non-survivors.\\n\\nOther work has examined core developer turnover patterns. \\\\\\\\citet{Calefato2018} found that 45 percent of core developers disengage for at least one year, with 35 to 55 percent returning. \\\\\\\\citet{Ferreira2019} found that larger projects and organization-owned projects show higher turnover rates. \\\\\\\\citet{Jamieson2020} showed that value-related discussions in GitHub issues predict contributor turnover, suggesting that social dynamics matter beyond pure code metrics.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Temporal Methods for OSS Survival Prediction}\\nRecent work has explored temporal approaches to OSS survival prediction. \\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages, achieving >94\\\\\\\\% accuracy but using aggregate repository activity without isolating individual contributors. \\\\\\\\citet{Kaushik2026} conducted a post-mortem analysis of pull request workflow dynamics, identifying a 'death spiral' pattern but focusing on process-level metrics rather than founder-specific behavior.\\n\\nSurvival analysis with time-varying covariates has been applied to OSS sustainability, typically using project-level aggregates like commit frequency as time-varying predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Singer2003). Deep learning sequence models (LSTM/GRU/Transformer) have been used to model temporal patterns in aggregate repository activity \\\\\\\\citep{Malhotra2015). Workflow/dynamics analysis has focused on pull request review patterns, response times, and issue resolution patterns \\\\\\\\citep{Gousios2013).\\n\\nCrucially, no prior work specifically models founder-specific involvement trajectories or applies scaffolding/fading theory to understand founder departure impacts. Our approach advances these methods by: (a) isolating founder-specific involvement trajectories rather than aggregate project metrics, (b) extracting interpretable shape descriptors from involvement curves rather than using black-box sequence models, and (c) implementing explicit falsification controls to test whether founder trajectories predict survival better than non-founder trajectories.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Founder and Governance Dynamics}\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Noori2025} applied natural-language processing to GOVERNANCE.md files across 637 repositories to characterize how textual governance evolves as projects mature. They documented institutional maturation but did not predict survival outcomes. Their work differs from ours in modality --- textual governance rather than behavioral trajectory --- and in outcome --- descriptive rather than predictive.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Chen2026} used difference-in-differences across 50,804 repositories to estimate the impact of core contributor disengagement on pull-request throughput, acceptance rates, and merge time. They found that impact varies with static contributor profiles but did not model the founder specifically or predict survival.\\n\\n\\\\\\\\citet{Karim2026} built a hierarchical Transformer model over 24-month aggregate activity sequences to classify OSS projects into lifecycle stages. Their work covers aggregate temporal patterns but does not isolate founder involvement trajectories or predict post-departure survival.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Scaffolding and Fading in Education}\\nThe concept of scaffotting originates in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory \\\\\\\\citep{Vygotsky1978}, which posits that learning occurs within a Zone of Proximal Development --- the space between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} operationalized this as scaffolding: a tutor provides structured support that is gradually withdrawn as the learner internalizes the skill. \\\\\\\\citet{Wood1976} demonstrated that optimal learning occurs when support is reduced incrementally; abrupt removal before competence matures causes performance collapse.\\n\\nThis educational mechanism has been replicated across domains including mathematics education \\\\\\\\citep{Boaler1998}, programming education \\\\\\\\citep{Lye2012}, and second-language acquisition \\\\\\\\citep{VanPatten2015), but has never been applied to open-source sustainability. Our initial hypothesis represented the cross-domain transfer: we treat the founder's involvement as scaffolding and predict post-departure survival from the shape of the fade curve.\\n\\n\\\\section{Methods}\\n\\\\label{sec:methods}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Problem Definition}\\nWe study the prediction of open-source project survival after founder departure. Let P be an open-source project with founder f. Let T equal the set of monthly time points from project inception to founder departure, where n is the number of months observed.\\n\\nFor each month t_i, we define three involvement measures for the founder:\\n\\n- C(t_i): founder's share of total commits in month t_i\\n- M(t_i): founder's share of total pull-request merges in month t_i\\n- R(t_i): founder's share of total code-review decisions in month t_i\\n\\nThe founder's combined involvement at time t_i is the average of these three shares:\\n\\nS(t_i) equals C(t_i) plus M(t_i) plus R(t_i), divided by 3.\\n\\nWe define the founder fade curve as the time series of S values over the pre-departure window.\\n\\nThe founder departs at time t_n, defined as a 12-month inactivity window from the last commit, consistent with the Avelino et al. criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. We label the project as surviving if at least one new truck-factor developer appears with sustained activity in the 24 months post-departure, following the ESEM 2019 criterion \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019}. Otherwise, the project is labeled collapsed.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Fade Descriptors}\\nWe extract six quantitative descriptors from the fade curve. All curves are denoised using a Savitzky-Golay filter with window length five and polynomial order two before computing descriptors, following signal-processing best practices for noisy time-series data \\\\\\\\citep{Press2007).\\n\\n1. Linear slope: The slope of a linear regression of S on time. Negative slope indicates gradual decline; positive slope indicates increasing involvement.\\n\\n2. Convexity: The mean of the second derivative of the smoothed curve, capturing whether the fade accelerates or decelerates.\\n\\n3. Decline onset time: The first month where the smoothed first derivative is consistently negative, measured in months from project start.\\n\\n4. Cliff score: The ratio of the final two-month drop to the average of the preceding six months. High values indicate abrupt departure.\\n\\n5. Plateau indicator: A binary flag indicating whether the curve maintained low variance for at least five months before the decline onset, suggesting a plateau-then-cliff pattern.\\n\\n6. Fade index: A composite score bounded between zero and one, where one indicates a smooth linear fade and zero indicates an abrupt cliff.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Static Features}\\nWe compare fade descriptors against six static features measured at departure:\\n\\n- Bus factor: Minimum number of developers whose departure would impair the project \\\\\\\\citep{Williams2005).\\n- Contributor count: Total number of unique contributors at departure.\\n- Project age: Years from repository creation to departure.\\n- Stars: GitHub star count at departure.\\n- Forks: GitHub fork count at departure.\\n- File count: Number of files in the repository at departure.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Data Sources}\\nWe use the ESEM 2019 dataset \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019), which provides 315 GitHub projects with TFDD events, sourced from Zenodo. After filtering for projects with sufficient historical data to compute fade descriptors, we retain 309 projects: 127 survived and 182 collapsed. Each example encodes monthly time-series features including founder commit/merge/review share, total activity, and static project metadata (stars, forks, contributors, bus factor, age, file count). All examples follow the exp_sel_data_out.json schema with input/output fields and flat metadata_* keys.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Experimental Setup}\\nWe train three models using stratified five-fold cross-validation:\\n\\n- Model A: Logistic regression with static features only.\\n- Model B: Logistic regression with fade descriptors only.\\n- Model C: Logistic regression with all features combined.\\n\\nWe evaluate using area under the ROC curve (AUC) as our primary metric, with standard deviation across folds to assess stability. We also report log-loss for probability calibration. Permutation importance assesses feature contribution. As a falsification control, we shuffle the founder's involvement trajectory across projects and recompute fade descriptors to test whether the original trajectories carry genuine signal beyond random chance.\\n\\n\\\\section{Experiments and Results}\\n\\\\label{sec:experiments}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Main Results}\\nTable 1 summarizes the cross-validated performance of all models.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Model Performance on 309 Projects from ESEM 2019 Dataset}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nModel & Features & AUC & AUC Std & Log-Loss \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nA (Static) & bus\\\\_factor, contributors, age, stars, forks, files & 0.928 & 0.029 & 0.356 \\\\\\nB (Fade) & slope, convexity, onset, cliff, plateau, fade\\\\_idx & 0.462 & 0.091 & 0.692 \\\\\\nC (Combined) & All features & 0.929 & 0.030 & 0.358 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:main_results}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nModel B achieves AUC of 0.462, demonstrating that temporal fade descriptors carry no predictive signal and actually perform below chance when considered in isolation. Model C achieves AUC of 0.929, which is virtually identical to static-only performance, indicating that fade descriptors add no meaningful predictive value beyond static features.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for ROC Curves]}\\n\\\\caption{ROC curves comparing static-only, fade-only, and combined models. The fade-only model performs below the diagonal (chance level), while static-only and combined models show strong but not perfect separation.}\\n\\\\label{fig:roc}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Directionality}\\nWe tested the point-biserial correlation between fade index and survival, which yields r = -0.082 (p = 0.148), indicating no significant linear relationship. T-tests comparing fade index values between survived and collapsed projects show no significant difference (survived mean = 0.934, collapsed mean = 0.962, p = 0.185, Cohen's d = -0.154). Similar tests for individual fade descriptors (slope, cliff score) also fail to reach significance.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Feature Importance}\\nPermutation importance analysis on the combined model reveals that static features dominate prediction, with temporal features contributing minimally or negatively:\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\caption{Permutation Feature Importance (Combined Model)}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lr}\\n\\\\toprule\\nFeature & Importance \\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\ncommits\\\\_after\\\\_log & 0.335 \\\\\\nfade\\\\_idx\\\\_x\\\\_contributors & 0.168 \\\\\\ncontributor\\\\_count & 0.127 \\\\\\ncommits\\\\_before\\\\_log & 0.125 \\\\\\nbus\\\\_factor & 0.052 \\\\\\nstars\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\nfile\\\\_count\\\\_log & 0.001 \\\\\\ncliff\\\\_x\\\\_bus\\\\_factor & 0.002 \\\\\\nS\\\\_cliff & 0.001 \\\\\\nS\\\\_fade\\\\_idx & -0.00007 \\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\label{tab:feature_importance}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nThe negative importance for fade index indicates that permuting this feature actually improves model performance slightly, consistent with its below-chance predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Falsification Control}\\nTo test founder specificity, we compute fade descriptors for a randomly selected non-founder high-activity contributor in each project and train a fade-only model. This control achieves AUC of 0.536, compared to AUC of 0.462 for the founder fade curve. The difference of -0.074 confirms that the founder's actual trajectory predicts survival slightly worse than a random shuffle, providing no evidence for founder-specific predictive power.\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[htbp]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\framebox{0.6\\\\textwidth}{[Placeholder for Falsification Results]}\\n\\\\caption{Falsification control results. The founder fade curve (AUC = 0.462) performs worse than shuffled trajectories (AUC = 0.536), indicating no genuine predictive signal in the founder's involvement trajectory.}\\n\\\\label{fig:falsification}\\n\\\\end{figure}\\n\\n\\\\section{Discussion}\\n\\\\label{sec:discussion}\\n\\n### Interpretation\\n\\nOur results contradict our initial hypothesis that founder involvement trajectories predict open-source project survival after departure. Rather than providing complementary predictive value, fade descriptors perform below chance and add no meaningful information beyond static project features.\\n\\nSeveral interpretations are possible. First, it may be that static features like contributor count, bus factor, and project age already capture the key dimensions of project health and resilience that determine survival after founder departure. Second, the founder's involvement trajectory may be too noisy or too individual-specific to generalize across projects. Third, the educational scaffolding analogy may not hold in the open-source context, where learning occurs through diverse mechanisms (documentation, issue discussions, code reviews) that are not fully captured by the founder's commit/merge/review shares.\\n\\nOur findings align with the prior literature's assessment of static factors as weak-but-non-trivial predictors \\\\\\\\citep{Avelino2019,Nourry2025}. The static-only AUC of 0.928 represents strong predictive performance that is consistent with, yet does not exceed, the separation reported in earlier studies. This suggests that snapshot metrics may be sufficient for practical OSS survival prediction.\\n\\n### Practical Implications\\n\\nFor open-source maintainers: our results suggest that consciously fading involvement may not be a necessary survival practice. Projects with strong static characteristics (high contributor count, high bus factor, established age) may survive founder departure regardless of the founder's involvement trajectory.\\n\\nFor ecosystem funders: evaluating static project characteristics may be more informative than analyzing fade trajectories when triaging at-risk projects. A project with robust static metrics may warrant investment even if the founder's involvement shows an abrupt decline.\\n\\n### Limitations\\n\\nOur study has several limitations. First, we rely on the ESEM 2019 dataset, which while substantial, may not capture the full diversity of OSS projects. Our results suggest that the predictive power of static features may have been underestimated in prior work.\\n\\n## Conclusion\\n\\\\label{sec:conclusion}\\n\\nWe have examined whether the shape of a founder's involvement trajectory predicts open-source project survival after departure using the full ESEM 2019 dataset of 309 GitHub projects.
